newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. says Cambodia must match talk with action.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Cambodia must match talk with action.

text.p: Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted his co-premier in a bloody takeover 10 days ago, said there will be an election in May but the United States said his democratic rhetoric must be matched by deeds.

In Phnom Penh a diplomatic source said on Wednesday there have been as many as 40 politically motivated killings in the wake of Hun Sen's ousting of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6.

The diplomatic source, who declined to be identified, said there was evidence some victims had been tortured, including four bodyguards of Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, who were found dead with their eyes gouged out.
Hun Sen told the Voice of America's Khmer language service in an interview late on Tuesday that he was implementing democracy.
"My party is like any other party and I hope on May 23, 1998, there will be an election and the election will be free, fair and right," Hun Sen said.
He added the National Assembly would be reconvened on July 28 and steps were under way to choose a replacement for Ranariddh as first prime minister.

Hun Sen said he thought relations with the United States, which suspended aid for 30 days in response to Ranariddh's ousting, were steady but Washington said on Tuesday it was unlikely to resume non-humanitarian aid to Cambodia.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing that Hun Sen's rhetoric in recent days, seemingly in favour of democracy, was not matched by action.
Washington allocated $35 million in aid to the Southeast Asian state for fiscal 1997, which ends in September.

Anticipating what might happen after 30 days, Burns said, "I know that we would very much like to keep going, keep operational those portions of the aid programme that benefit people but not the government.

"I don't think you'll see us embracing Hun Sen and giving him billions of dollars, or millions of dollars, for his own personal use ... I don't anticipate you'll see a lot of government-to-government aid (from the United States to Cambodia)."

Referring to reports of widespread human rights abuses in Cambodia, Burns said: "(Hun Sen's) words are beautiful over the past 48 hours ... but whether or not he can match those words in reality with his actions is a very big test for him."

The diplomatic source in Phnom Penh said that while attacks on officials from Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party appeared to be going on across the country, the figure of 40 deaths had been compiled mostly from incidents in the Phnom Penh area. It was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge.

"It's very unclear if this is a centrally orchestrated, carefully planned purge or more dispersed -- a general uncoordinated attack on FUNCINPEC officials," he said. "But even if it is the latter, it could be stopped."
King Norodom Sihanouk on Tuesday accused Hun Sen's police and troops of torturing and killing political opponents and urged an end to the bloodshed.

"I am profoundly distressed at the reports that the military and members of the national police have cruelly tortured and killed without mercy their enemies after having arrested or captured them," Sihanouk said in a letter sent from Beijing to Chea Sim, the acting head of state, in Phnom Penh.
Military officials denied detainees were being mistreated and said they were undergoing "re-education".

Sihanouk, who is in Beijing for medical treatment, urged that those detained or arrested as enemies of the state be treated in line with the law, as well as in accordance with provisions of relevant international treaties to which Cambodia is a signatory.
